paragraphs.text: Lesson 8. A brand new smartphone.
Listen to this conversation between Kate and Mandy, two high school students.
First, try to answer the comprehension questions as you listen, then learn the expressions.
Check it out! We have my very own smartphone!
Cool! I can't believe your parents just dished out the money for a brand new phone.
I thought you were in trouble for bombing your algebra test.
I was, but my mom and dad made a deal with me.
They'll pay for my smartphone if I bring home good grades.
I've got another shot at the algebra test.
Mrs. Smith is gonna let me retake it next Tuesday.
If I pass, I keep my smartphone. If I fail, then my parents will confiscate my phone until I bring my grades up.
So, basically, they're bribing you to study.
Yeah, in a way, I have to admit, their little scheme is working though.
Last night, I studied for two hours straight.
I really want to keep my smartphone. Otherwise, I'll be totally out of the loop.
I know what you mean. Ever since I started working for the school paper, I've had to be on call 24-7.
The editor, Sarah, is constantly texting the article ideas, sharing picks, changing plans for the next issue on the fly.
If I didn't have my smartphone, she'd probably kick me off the team.
At least you bought your smartphone with your own allowance,
so you don't have to worry about it being taken away.
My dad just doesn't get how important it is to have a phone.
You feel like totally left out without one.
Your dad's from a different generation and just sees things differently. That's all.
Believe me, I know. My parents have given me sermons about the good old days when people weren't so hooked on technology.
Well, who says the good old days were better? I can text you in a second compared to waiting a week for you to get a letter in the mail.
I can listen to music and check my email anywhere I go. I can download tons of cool apps.
I can- Hey, you're preaching on the choir, girl. I love my phone, too. But you've got to admit, our parents have a point.
When my dad was a kid, he played outside, and today I never see kids outside playing.
Yeah, I guess.
My little brother can't tear himself away from his new playstation. When his friends come over, they just hold up in his room and play for hours.
Just imagine what life will be like for our own kids someday. They'll probably have, I don't know, virtual reality or telepathy or something like that.
And smartphones will be considered primitive.
Geez, Mandy, just let me enjoy having my smartphone for now.
Okay, okay. Go enjoy your phone. Ah, just got a message from Sarah, so I gotta run. Text me later.
Let's learn the vocabulary from today's conversation about smartphones.
When Kate shows Mandy her new phone, Mandy says, I can't believe your parents just dished out the money for a brand new phone.
The phrasal verb dished out means gave freely without restraint.
Mandy then says, I thought you were in trouble for bombing your algebra test.
The word bombing is slang. It means doing very badly on something. In this case, failing the test.
Kate says she was in trouble, but her mom and dad made a deal with her. Made a deal simply means made an agreement.
And Kate says, I've got another shot at the algebra test. Another shot means another try or another attempt.
Another opportunity to do it. If Kate fails the test on Tuesday, then her parents will confiscate her phone.
The word confiscate means to take possession of something by authority. Usually it's the police or someone official who confiscates items or evidence, which might help in solving a crime.
Mandy replies, basically, they are bribing you to study. The word bribe is a verb meaning to offer a reward or give a reward in order to influence someone to act a certain way.

A bribe is seen as something dishonest. For example, if a police officer catches you speeding and you offer the police officer $50 to forget about it and not write you a ticket, that's a bribe, and it's illegal.
But in this case, the deal between Kate and her parents is not illegal. Her parents are offering her a reward in order to influence her behavior, in order to try to get her to study in this case.
Kate says, I have to admit their little scheme is working. A scheme is a secret or devious plan. Kate says she really wants to keep her smartphone, otherwise she'll be totally out of the loop.
The expression out of the loop means not knowing or not being involved in the situation.
Mandy says she understands, ever since she started working for the school paper, she's had to be on call 24-7.
On call means available if called for, and 24-7 refers to 24 hours in a day and seven days a week. In other words, Mandy has to be available all the time.
The editor of the school newspaper, Sarah, is constantly changing plans for the next issue on the fly.
On the fly means spontaneously, without previous planning.
If Mandy didn't have a smartphone, Sarah would probably kick her off the team. This means to expel or force Mandy to leave the team.
Kate says, at least you bought your smartphone with your own allowance. The word allowance refers to a small amount of money that parents regularly give their children.
Kate's dad just doesn't get how important it is to have a phone. Doesn't get is a slang way to say doesn't understand.
Some people, when they want to say, I don't understand something, they say, I don't get it.
Kate says she feels totally left out without a smartphone. Left out means excluded socially.
Mandy's parents have also given her sermons about the good old days.
This expression, to give someone a sermon, means to give the person a long speech or lecture that's usually intended to prove a point or influence their behavior.
The word sermon is used for the lecture which is given in church, but in this case it's not talking about a religious context.
It's simply talking about a long speech.
Mandy's parents have given her sermons about the good old days when people weren't so hooked on technology.
Hooked on means addicted to.
Kate starts talking about all the different reasons she loves her smartphone, and Mandy says,
Hey, you're preaching to the choir girl.
Preaching to the choir means trying to convince someone who already agrees with you.
Kate talks about her little brother.
She says, My little brother can't tear himself away from his new PlayStation.
If you can't tear yourself away from something, it means that thing is so addictive or you're so involved in it that you can't manage to stop or you can't manage to get away from it.
When Kate's brother's friends come over, they just hole up in his room and play for hours.
The phrasal verb, hole up means to hide or take shelter.
Mandy imagines what life will be like for the next generation.
She says they'll probably have virtual reality or telepathy.
Telepathy refers to the ability to communicate mentally through transmitting thoughts.
And Mandy says, In the future, smartphones will be considered primitive.
The word primitive means old, basic, not sophisticated or modern.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
